items.title: On-Device Anomaly Detection: Statistical Baselines vs. Learned Models
items.summary: There is a reflex in IoT projects that goes: "we have anomaly data, so we need a model." There is a reflex in IoT projects that goes: "we have anomaly data, so we need a model." Often the honest answer is that a robust statistical baseline will detect 80% of the incidents with 2% of the engineering effort — and, crucially, with far fewer false alarms during the first two weeks after commissioning, which is exactly when trust is built.

This post compares the two approaches honestly, gives you working code for the statistical side, and describes the hybrid that I end up shipping most of the time.

What "anomaly" means operationally

Before comparing detectors, define what you are detecting. Three very different problems get called "anomaly detection":

  1. Point outliers — a single sample outside the historical range. Sensor glitch, transient spike.
  2. Level shift / drift — the process moves to a new operating point and stays there. Fouling, wear, a changed setpoint.
  3. Shape change — the signal's dynamics change while its mean stays flat. Bearing defect, looseness, cavitation.

A robust z-score handles (1) well and (2) adequately. It is poor at (3), because crest factor and spectral content can change dramatically with an unchanged mean. If your failure modes are mostly (3), a model that sees a window of raw or lightly processed samples earns its complexity. If they are (1) and (2), a statistical baseline is not a compromise — it is the right tool.

The baseline, properly done

A naive mean ± 3σ fails for three reasons: spikes inflate σ, the distribution is rarely Gaussian, and it ignores time. Fix all three:

import numpy as np

class RobustBaseline:
    """Median/MAD baseline with EWMA smoothing and hysteresis.

    Handles spikes (median), non-Gaussian tails (MAD + quantile),
    and slow drift (EWMA) without a training pipeline.
    """

    MAD_TO_SIGMA = 1.4826

    def __init__(self, alpha=0.02, warmup=300, k_warn=4.0, k_alarm=6.0, hold=5):
        self.alpha = alpha
        self.warmup = warmup
        self.k_warn = k_warn
        self.k_alarm = k_alarm
        self.hold = hold
        self.n = 0
        self.med = None
        self.mad = None
        self.state = "ok"
        self._over = 0

    def update(self, x: float) -> tuple[str, float]:
        if self.med is None:
            self.med, self.mad = x, 1e-6
        self.n += 1

        # EWMA on centre and spread: adapts to setpoint changes, resists spikes
        self.med += self.alpha * (x - self.med)
        self.mad += self.alpha * (abs(x - self.med) - self.mad)

        sigma = max(self.mad * self.MAD_TO_SIGMA, 1e-9)
        z = (x - self.med) / sigma

        # during warm-up, only widen the band; never alert
        if self.n < self.warmup:
            return "warmup", z

        if abs(z) >= self.k_alarm:
            self._over += 1
        else:
            self._over = 0

        if self._over >= self.hold:
            self.state = "alarm"
        elif abs(z) >= self.k_warn:
            self.state = "warn"
        elif self.state == "alarm" and abs(z) < self.k_warn:
            self.state = "warn"
        elif abs(z) < self.k_warn * 0.5:
            self.state = "ok"
        return self.state, z

Four design choices carry most of the value:

  • EWMA rather than a fixed historical window. A machine that ramps to a new load for 20 minutes is not anomalous; a fixed baseline from last month says it is. The EWMA follows the operating point.
  • MAD rather than σ. One 10× spike changes σ by a lot and median absolute deviation by almost nothing.
  • A warm-up period that never alerts. You will thank yourself on day one of every deployment.
  • Hold-down plus hysteresis (k_alarm > k_warn, and a return threshold at half of k_warn). This alone typically cuts alert volume by half. More on that in the hysteresis post.
Where the baseline breaks

Three failure modes are worth knowing because they tell you when to graduate to a model:

Correlated channels. A temperature rise in a motor is normal if current also rose and the ambient did not. A per-channel z-score cannot express "high, but consistent with load". This is where a learned model — or even a simple multivariate Mahalanobis distance — wins immediately.

Shape-only faults. A crest-factor rise from 2.1 to 3.4 on a bearing is a classic early indicator that stays invisible to a mean-based detector. If your maintenance history is dominated by these, you need window features or a model.

Multi-modal normal behaviour. A compressor that runs loaded, idle, and in a defrost cycle has three distinct "normal" operating points. A single centre/spread pair produces alerts at every transition. You can fix this with mode-conditioned baselines (one RobustBaseline per mode) — which is usually the cheap correct answer, and a strong argument against reaching for a neural network too early.

Fair comparison: the metrics that matter

Do not compare detectors with AUC. Compare them the way operations experiences them:

  • Time to detect — minutes from fault onset to first alarm, per incident.
  • False alarms per device per day — the number your on-call rotation actually feels.
  • Alert precision — share of alarms a technician judges actionable.
  • Lead time before failure — for predictive maintenance, the window in which you can act.

A worked comparison table from a real fleet of 180 pumps looked like this:

Detector Median time to detect False alarms / device / day Precision Flash need Per-channel robust z 41 min 1.8 0.34 < 1 KB Multivariate Mahalanobis 22 min 0.9 0.52 ~ 2 KB 1D CNN on raw window 8 min 0.4 0.71 96 KB CNN + rule engine + dedup 8 min 0.1 0.88 96 KB

Note the last row: the big win in precision did not come from a better model, it came from the rule engine and de-duplication layered on top. That pattern repeats — the model is rarely the whole answer.

The Mahalanobis row is worth dwelling on. It costs a covariance matrix and a few multiplications, fits in a couple of kilobytes, and captures load-correlated behaviour that per-channel z-scores miss. For many fleets it is the best effort-to-value ratio available.

import numpy as np

class MahalanobisBaseline:
    def __init__(self, feature_names, shrink=0.10):
        self.names = feature_names
        self.shrink = shrink
        self.mu = None
        self.inv_cov = None

    def fit(self, X: np.ndarray) -> "MahalanobisBaseline":
        self.mu = X.mean(axis=0)
        cov = np.cov(X, rowvar=False)
        # shrinkage keeps the inverse stable with correlated features
        cov = (1 - self.shrink) * cov + self.shrink * np.eye(cov.shape[0]) * np.trace(cov) / cov.shape[0]
        self.inv_cov = np.linalg.inv(cov)
        return self

    def score(self, x: np.ndarray) -> float:
        d = x - self.mu
        return float(np.sqrt(d @ self.inv_cov @ d))

Score thresholds come from the chi-square distribution, not from a 3σ rule: for d features, the 99.9th percentile of χ²(d) is a defensible alarm threshold. Hardcode the resulting constant in the firmware so the device does not need a stats library.

The hybrid I usually ship 
per-sample   → device: hard limits (deterministic, no model)
per-window   → gateway: robust baseline per operating mode  (cheap, always on)
               └─ if |z| > k_warn: run the learned model on the window
per-event    → cloud: correlation, dedup, triage

The baseline acts as a cheap gate, and the model runs only on windows the baseline flagged. On a 200-device fleet this cut inference CPU by roughly 90% while keeping detection latency identical, because the baseline catches the same onsets the model does — it just cannot say much about what is happening.

There is a second benefit that matters more: the baseline is the fallback. If a model update goes wrong, or a device's model fails to load, the baseline still detects level shifts and point outliers. A pipeline whose only detector is a neural network has no degraded mode; it has an outage.

Guarding the baseline against setpoint changes

Baselines go bad when the process changes: a new product run, a retuned controller, a replaced sensor. Three cheap guards:

1 Mode-conditioned state. Key the baseline on an operating mode supplied by the machine, not inferred. baselines[mode].update(x).
2 Commissioning reset with an explicit window. Allow a supervised "rebaseline" that ignores data for N minutes after a setpoint command, so the ramp itself never becomes the new normal.
3 Slow-drift detection on the baseline itself. Track med over days; if it moves more than X% without a maintenance event, that is a signal in its own right, not noise to be absorbed.

That third guard is genuinely useful. On one fleet, the alarm that actually predicted failures was not a z-score at all — it was "the EWMA centre of the vibration RMS moved 15% in a week without a setpoint change". Slow, boring, and more predictive than the model.

Deciding

Use the baseline alone when: your failure modes are point outliers or level shifts, you have fewer than ~10 correlated channels, and your false-alarm budget is tight from day one.

Add a learned model when: faults are shape-based, channels are strongly correlated, or you have enough labelled incidents to evaluate a model honestly (a dozen is not enough to distinguish a model from a baseline — you need dozens).

Ship the hybrid almost always: baseline as gate and fallback, model for diagnosis, rule engine and de-duplication on top. That is the architecture the rest of this series builds toward.

items.title: GPT-6.2 Sol: 38% cheaper, 87 Elo points worse
items.summary: GPT-6.2 Sol: 38% cheaper, 87 Elo points worse GPT-6.2 Sol reasons about four times less than its predecessor and lost roughly 87 Elo points doing it. GPT-6.2 Astra got cheaper too — and kept its Elo. OpenAI sold both models the same way: fewer tokens, same quality. Independent battle data says that was true for exactly one of them. The claim A post on micjm.com this week ("OpenAI may be in cost control mode," Hacker News, 215 points) argues that the GPT-6.2 pair was tuned for cost savings: output tokens per task and reasoning tokens per task both dropped versus GPT-6 and GPT-6.1. The evidence comes from AgentDuel, a blind coding-agent battle system — two models get the same prompt, tools, and system prompt in a fork of OpenCode 2.3.2, a human picks the winner without knowing which is which, and all votes are fitted with Bradley–Terry on the Elo scale. 18 models have 100+ eligible votes. The p-values are the hard part of the claim, and they're exact, from the post's text: metric Sol 6.1 -> 6.2 Astra 6 -> 6.2 output tokens p = 0.0055 p = 0.022 reasoning tokens p = 0.00013 p = 0.0064 Both models think less, and for Sol the reasoning drop is significant at p = 0.00013. That is not noise. How much less, read off the charts The post's charts plot each model's median tokens per task against its opponents' median on the same tasks. I read the values off the published PNGs, so treat these as approximate: reasoning tokens/task (median, model vs opponents' median) Astra 6 ~1,400 vs ~2,900 Astra 6.2 ~1,400 vs ~5,700 Sol 6.1 ~1,200 vs ~3,000 Sol 6.2 ~300 vs ~5,700 output tokens/task (median, model vs opponents' median) Astra 6 ~5,400 vs ~7,200 Astra 6.2 ~6,600 vs ~13,200 Sol 6.1 ~4,400 vs ~7,200 Sol 6.2 ~3,300 vs ~15,400 Sol 6.2's median reasoning fell to roughly a quarter of Sol 6.1's, while its opponents on the same tasks were reasoning ~5,700 tokens. Astra 6.2's reasoning held flat against its predecessor. Both 6.2 models sit far below the "equal token counts" diagonal — they are the outliers in a field of 18 models, and the only two that moved that far down in one generation. What the Elo did The cost chart in the same post plots Elo against median cost per task relative to opponents: model Elo (blog snapshot) median cost vs opponents Sol 6.1 ~982 0.81x Sol 6.2 ~895 0.50x Astra 6 ~983 5.7x Astra 6.2 ~988 3.6x Sol got 38% cheaper relative to the models it faced (0.81x to 0.50x) and gave back ~87 Elo. Astra got 37% cheaper relative to its opponents (5.7x to 3.6x) and gave back nothing — Elo ~983 to ~988, flat. The live leaderboard complicates the Sol number in an honest way: regenerated November 27, 00:00 UTC, it shows GPT-6.2 Sol at rank 12 with Elo 936 (+54/−59), $0.43 per task, 1.7 minutes per task. That is higher than the blog snapshot's ~895, and the ±55 confidence interval means the drop from ~982 is within noise at the leaderboard level. So the Elo story is: Sol is down somewhere between ~50 and ~90 points depending on the snapshot, with wide error bars. The token story is the solid one — the p-values don't have that problem. For scale, the same leaderboard has Qwen 4 Max at rank 5, Elo 1007, $0.34 per task, and Grok 4.7 at rank 11, Elo 939, $0.79 per task. What OpenAI said at launch OpenAI shipped GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol on November 17, and sold both on cost per task as much as on scores. Astra's list prices fell 20% versus GPT-6 Astra ($10 to $8 input, $50 to $40 output per million tokens; cached input down 60% to $0.40). Sol's prices did not change: $2 input, $0.10 cached, $10 output per million, same as GPT-6.1 Sol. The launch pitch was that both models do better work with fewer tokens: Astra up 5.2 points on Agents' Last Exam at under a third of the cost, up 9 points on Terminal-Bench-Science at under a third of the cost. Against the independent data, that pitch splits in half. For Astra it holds: same Elo, a third less relative cost. For Sol it doesn't: the price list never changed, the tokens fell, and so did the Elo. "Talks less" is only a win if the talking that got cut wasn't doing work. The usage-limits rumor, revisited In my code-golf piece this morning I noted an unverified X post claiming OpenAI cut GPT-6.2 usage limits, with Astra hitting its limits 40% faster. This data gives that rumor a plausible mechanism — a model that burns fewer tokens per task should stretch a cap, not hit it faster — but it does not verify or refute the limits claim itself. Caps are a billing decision, tokens are a model behavior, and the two can move in opposite directions. The limits claim stays unverified. What this means if you use them If you pay per token, 6.2 is cheaper per task for both models — Astra strictly, Sol with an asterisk. If you pay per month with a usage cap, fewer tokens per task should buy you more tasks, which is presumably the point of the tuning. But Sol's trade is real: you are getting a worse model for less money per task, and whether that's a good deal depends on whether you grade on Elo or on dollars. Astra is the free lunch here; Sol is the discount shelf. Caveats, stated plainly The token medians and Elo figures from the blog's charts are values I read off the published PNGs — approximate, not from a data file. AgentDuel is a community benchmark: 18 models with 100+ eligible votes each, blind voting, Bradley–Terry Elo, with wide confidence intervals (±55 on Sol's live Elo). I did not run the battles myself. OpenAI's launch numbers (Agents' Last Exam, Terminal-Bench-Science, price cuts) are vendor claims from the November 17 announcement, not independent measurements. The usage-limits claim remains a single unverified X post. Sources micjm.com, "OpenAI may be in cost control mode," November 26, 2026: https://micjm.com/blog/openai-is-in-cost-control-mode/ AgentDuel leaderboard (generated November 27, 2026, 00:00 UTC): https://agentduel.com/leaderboard OpenAI GPT-6.2 Astra/Sol launch pricing and benchmarks, November 17, 2026 (via Eden AI summary of OpenAI's announcement): https://www.edenai.co/post/gpt-6-2-astra-vs-sol-routing Hacker News thread, "OpenAI may be in cost control mode," 215 points, November 26, 2026: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50652527

items.title: 23 or 30 tools? Google's Gmail MCP can't decide
items.summary: 23 or 30 tools? Google's Gmail MCP can't decide I asked Google's Gmail MCP server what tools it has, 30 times in 11 seconds. 18 times it said 23 tools. 12 times it said 30 — including send_message , reply , and forward . Same endpoint, same request, two different answers. The setup On November 24, Google made its eight hosted Workspace MCP servers generally available — Gmail, Drive, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Calendar, Chat, and Tasks — and published a new Workspace AI Tools Addendum. From February 1, 2027, any tool "driven by an AI Agent" must reach Workspace through those servers instead of calling the REST APIs directly. Agents that keep calling REST get capped at Standard Tier quotas no matter what they pay for. The headline limitation, reported everywhere this week, is that the Gmail server can't send email: it searches, reads, drafts, and labels, but send, reply, forward, and editing drafts are partner-only. Google's own developer release notes describe the Gmail MCP server the same way — search and read, create and retrieve drafts, manage labels, trash and spam. No send. I wanted to check that claim against the live server. The servers answer tools/list without an OAuth token, so the catalog is public. I probed all eight. What the eight servers advertise server endpoint tools (no auth) gmail gmailmcp.googleapis.com/mcp/v1 23 or 30 <- flip-flops drive drivemcp.googleapis.com/mcp/v1 9 docs docsmcp.googleapis.com/mcp/v1 2 sheets sheetsmcp.googleapis.com/mcp/v1 6 slides slidesmcp.googleapis.com/mcp/v1 4 calendar calendarmcp.googleapis.com/mcp/v1 9 chat chatmcp.googleapis.com/mcp/v1 4 tasks tasksmcp.googleapis.com/mcp/v1 9 Seven of the eight are rock stable. Gmail is not. The flip-flop, measured My first tools/list call to Gmail hung — the server never closed the SSE stream. Sending initialize first fixed it (HTTP 200 in 0.42s, server identifies as StatelessServer , version ESF ). After that, plain tools/list calls answered in ~0.3–0.6s. Then I ran the same request 30 times in a row, 11.0 seconds total: response count raw bytes send_message present? 23 tools 18 88,436 no 30 tools 12 149,735 yes The 30-tool answer always adds exactly the same 7 tools: send_message, reply, forward, update_draft, create_filter, list_filters, update_label I checked whether the answer depends on what I send. It doesn't — at least not on anything I varied. I alternated the MCP-Protocol-Version header across 2025-03-26 , 2025-06-18 , 2024-11-05 , 2025-11-25 , and no header at all, 12 calls: every group returned a mix. Drive, probed 10 times for comparison, returned 9 tools all 10 times. The flip-flop is Gmail-specific, server-side, and not header-driven. The boring explanation is load balancing across backends on different rollout versions; the interesting one is a staged rollout in progress. Either way, the catalog you get depends on which backend answers. One more detail: Google's Gmail quotas page lists eight partner-only tools — the seven above plus delete_label . delete_label never appeared in either variant. So the live catalog holds 7 of the 8 gated tools, and the documented public set is the 23-tool one. The 88,436-byte figure matches the 23-tool count published earlier this week exactly — that measurement was real, it was just one side of a coin flip. What I could not test Calling any tool without authentication returns the same error for public and gated tools alike: HTTP 401 "Request is missing required authentication credential. Expected OAuth 2 access token, login cookie or other valid authentication credential." create_draft , send_message , and search_threads all fail identically, so I cannot tell from outside whether send_message actually executes for a non-partner with a valid token — Google's docs say it requires partner access, and I did not test with real credentials, because testing send means sending a real email. The honest statement is narrower than the headlines: the catalog is inconsistent, and the documentation says send is gated. Whether the gate holds at call time is untested by me. Why this matters before February 1 If your agent checks capabilities once at startup — the normal thing to do — it can conclude Gmail can send email, or that it can't, depending on which backend answered that one request. On November 24, Google made its eight hosted Workspace MCP servers generally available — Gmail, Drive, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Calendar, Chat, and Tasks — and published a new Workspace AI Tools Addendum. Agents that keep calling REST get capped at Standard Tier quotas no matter what they pay for.

The headline limitation, reported everywhere this week, is that the Gmail server can't send email: it searches, reads, drafts, and labels, but send, reply, forward, and editing drafts are partner-only. Google's own developer release notes describe the Gmail MCP server the same way — search and read, create and retrieve drafts, manage labels, trash and spam. No send.

What the eight servers advertise 
server     endpoint                          tools (no auth)
gmail      gmailmcp.googleapis.com/mcp/v1    23 or 30  <- flip-flops
drive      drivemcp.googleapis.com/mcp/v1    9
docs       docsmcp.googleapis.com/mcp/v1     2
sheets     sheetsmcp.googleapis.com/mcp/v1   6
slides     slidesmcp.googleapis.com/mcp/v1   4
calendar   calendarmcp.googleapis.com/mcp/v1 9
chat       chatmcp.googleapis.com/mcp/v1     4
tasks      tasksmcp.googleapis.com/mcp/v1    9

items.summary: For a small media app, tenant isolation changes the storage decision more than a headline storage rate. Backblaze B2, Cloudflare R2, AWS S3, and Wasabi can all look attractive for backups until an EU or US customer needs a private, audited restore. Short answer: compare the full restore path (requests, egress, and integration work) across Backblaze B2, Cloudflare R2, AWS S3, and Wasabi; choose the provider whose private-link and regional behavior matches your recovery test, then keep a second copy outside that bucket. Infrai is worth testing alongside those four when a Node.js cron worker needs private uploads and expiring restore links through plain HTTP. Its storage calls use the same bearer-key convention as other backend capabilities, so the comparison includes integration effort, not only provider meters. The experiment: model a real restore, not a storage invoice I model one nightly Node.js job per tenant. It writes compressed Postgres dumps and media manifests, keeps objects private, and issues a download URL that expires after a support engineer confirms the tenant. The test has two measurements: the monthly write footprint and the cost and latency of restoring one tenant in the EU and one in the US. The expensive surprise usually appears after the happy-path upload. Imagine a support ticket from a US tenant while the only copy sits in an EU region: the restore script may make a list request, fetch a manifest, download hundreds of segments, retry a timed-out object, and then send the archive through your own API for audit logging. Each hop has a meter or a CPU bill. I would capture those steps as separate counters, tag them with tenant and region, and repeat the run with a 10-minute presigned URL and with a 15-minute URL. That gives a useful upper bound for an incident, including the case where an engineer has to restart halfway through. It also exposes an isolation mistake early: if a fixture for tenant 42 can ever resolve a key under tenant 43, the test should fail before any price comparison is discussed. The simple approach is one shared bucket with a tenant prefix. It is easy to operate, but a prefix is a naming convention, not an isolation boundary. A better baseline uses a bucket policy or credential scope per tenant (where the provider supports it), plus server-side checks that bind the requested key to the authenticated tenant. The restore endpoint returns a short-lived presigned URL; the browser never receives a long-lived secret. That distinction matters for small SaaS budgets. A restore can touch thousands of objects, and API request charges or cross-region transfer can outweigh the gigabytes stored. I would run the same scripted restore twice, from an EU worker and a US worker, and record bytes, request count, elapsed time, and failed-link rate before declaring a winner. Your mileage may vary with object size and support traffic. Measure first. Can app backups stay private across Backblaze, Cloudflare, AWS, and Wasabi? Its broader platform puts storage and adjacent backend calls behind one key and one bill, which removes credential and invoice plumbing for a solo team. I would try Infrai for teams that value a single integration boundary and can enforce tenant authorization in their own service. Where this choice is the wrong tool There is a hard boundary. items.summary: I wrote this as part of the Kiroween 2026 hackathon (Frankenstein category). One field renamed in an MCP server. The server's tests were updated with it, so they stay green. A caller that still reads total finds it gone. That is the failure I wanted to catch before shipping, and I wanted to catch it using what an agent actually called , not what the server says it can do. This is a write-up of what worked, what the obvious check missed, and one result that found nothing. The obvious check sees too little The demo server (hollow-inn, ours) has three versions. v2 carries three breaks I planted on purpose: quote renames total to total_cents , search_rooms changes a default limit, and cancel_booking becomes booking_cancel . An input-schema diff of tools/list (tools removed, added, inputSchema changed) reports 2 changes : the removed cancel_booking and the added booking_cancel . The quote rename and the search_rooms default are invisible to it, because neither touches an input schema. Replaying ten recorded calls against v2: HOLD · 4 rattled, 1 cracked · 10 jars compared · 4 of 6 tools · not recorded: booking_cancel, get_room SPC-0002 · quote · rattled · /total, /total_cents · suspected rename from /total ×100 SPC-0010 · search_rooms · rattled · /rooms, /rooms/r-08, /rooms/r-09 · - SPC-0009 · cancel_booking · cracked · - · tool not in tools/list ( evidence/replay/racks-vs-v2.txt , trimmed) Five of ten recorded calls came back different, four of them in tools whose inputs never changed. That is the whole argument for replaying calls instead of diffing schemas. Capture from inside the agent The calls come from real Kiro CLI sessions. A pair of Kiro hooks, PreToolUse and PostToolUse , each with a per-server @hollowinn matcher, see the tool input and response from inside the agent, so there is no proxy and no change to the server. The PostToolUse half: { "name" : "specimen-jar-post" , "trigger" : "PostToolUse" , "matcher" : "@hollowinn" , "action" : { "type" : "command" , "command" : "npx --no-install specimen hook post --server hollowinn" } } The PreToolUse half ( specimen-jar-pre.json ) runs the same command with hook pre . The CLI is not published to npm: run npx specimen from a clone of the repo after npm ci . Each call is sealed as a jar : request and response text byte for byte, redacted on write, checksummed. The hook costs p50 465 / 474 ms (pre / post) per call (CLI wall-clock) over 30 fresh npx processes per hook on my laptop ( evidence/bench/hook.md ), excluding Kiro's own hook launch. Closing the loop A red jar goes to a Kiro custom agent that may only write under .kiro/specs/ ; it files a bugfix spec with the captured call as the repro, and a deterministic check-spec accepts or rejects it. Kiro's Bug Fix workflow then designs the fix and executes its implementation tasks (for two specs I ran the final acceptance steps myself). After three specs, v2.1 replays SHIP, 10 of 10 . Three of those jars carry one new compatible field; --strict calls that HOLD. The null result Run against a server I did not write ( @modelcontextprotocol/server-memory 1.0.0 to 2.2.1), the replay found no break: HOLD, 3 preserved, 2 unsealed. The two unsealed ones exist because that server also returns structuredContent that a text-only jar cannot compare. That is a limit of my jar format, not a clean bill for the server. What I would not claim Not the first MCP record/replay tool (mcp-recorder, AgentVCR and mcpsnoop exist). Ten jars, five of six tools; SHIP means "clean on the recorded set". The breaks are mine. No outside user has run it yet. Live cabinet (replays in your browser): https://specimen.edycu.dev/ · Code (MIT): https://github.com/edycutjong/specimen · Built for Kiroween 2026 (Frankenstein).

The calls come from real Kiro CLI sessions. A pair of Kiro hooks, PreToolUse and PostToolUse, each with a per-server @hollowinn matcher, see the tool input and response from inside the agent, so there is no proxy and no change to the server. The PostToolUse half:

{
  "name": "specimen-jar-post",
  "trigger": "PostToolUse",
  "matcher": "@hollowinn",
  "action": { "type": "command", "command": "npx --no-install specimen hook post --server hollowinn" }
}

The PreToolUse half (specimen-jar-pre.json) runs the same command with hook pre. The CLI is not published to npm: run npx specimen from a clone of the repo after npm ci.

Each call is sealed as a jar: request and response text byte for byte, redacted on write, checksummed. The hook costs p50 465 / 474 ms (pre / post) per call (CLI wall-clock) over 30 fresh npx processes per hook on my laptop (evidence/bench/hook.md), excluding Kiro's own hook launch.

Closing the loop

A red jar goes to a Kiro custom agent that may only write under .kiro/specs/; it files a bugfix spec with the captured call as the repro, and a deterministic check-spec accepts or rejects it. Kiro's Bug Fix workflow then designs the fix and executes its implementation tasks (for two specs I ran the final acceptance steps myself). After three specs, v2.1 replays SHIP, 10 of 10. Three of those jars carry one new compatible field; --strict calls that HOLD.

The null result

Run against a server I did not write (@modelcontextprotocol/server-memory 1.0.0 to 2.2.1), the replay found no break: HOLD, 3 preserved, 2 unsealed. The two unsealed ones exist because that server also returns structuredContent that a text-only jar cannot compare. That is a limit of my jar format, not a clean bill for the server.

What I would not claim

Not the first MCP record/replay tool (mcp-recorder, AgentVCR and mcpsnoop exist). Ten jars, five of six tools; SHIP means "clean on the recorded set". The breaks are mine. No outside user has run it yet.

items.title: LIMBO: offline apps that show you the edit they could not merge
items.summary: I wrote this as part of the Kiroween 2026 hackathon (Skeleton Crew category). The angle: a merge that loses an edit silently is worse than one that fails At a lake with no signal, Sari ticks "tent" on a shared packing list while a friend deletes it. Back in range, one edit wins and the other disappears. Nobody can tell which. Last-write-wins is the default and it hides the loss. LIMBO is a small local-first skeleton where every operation declares how it merges , plus two apps built on it. When two offline edits genuinely conflict, the loser does not vanish: the deleted tent comes back as a ghost twin beside the ticked one, and one tap resolves it. What is measured, and what is not Convergence is property-tested, not proven: 3 replicas, 10,000 random orderings, seed 20251031, 0 divergences ( evidence/convergence/full-2026-11-22.json ). The suite has a vacuity guard and mutation fixtures that must fail, because a property test that cannot fail proves nothing. A judge can press Run shuffle test in the live app and watch their own browser replay the on-screen ops in random causal orders (a replay of what is on screen, not the 10,000-ordering run). One thing no CRDT can do: stop two offline users both claiming the last stove. LIMBO makes claims provisional, picks one claimant by a declared rule on reconnect, and shows the other person their lost claim. How Kiro built it Claude Code orchestrated: it wrote each brief, launched a headless Kiro CLI session, reviewed the diff and committed. Kiro wrote the specs and executed the tasks: 194 Kiro sessions (679.87 credits; 179 across 12 specs, 15 kit and bootstrap), 115 of 124 product commits carrying a Kiro session trailer (92.74%); 17 ledger rows are edits made outside Kiro (9 of the 124 product commits), listed in the repo. The kit: 6 steering files, 2 custom agents, 8 hooks (1,824 logged fires) and a convergence MCP server. The part I liked most is an Agent Stop hook that blocks "done" while the properties fail, and hands Kiro the shrunk counterexample. It blocked 2 times: once on a property suite that ran a new op without its payload generator (Kiro wired it in), once on a fault I seeded on purpose. The honest part I pre-registered an A/B: same op-writing task with and without the kit, 20 runs. Result: 0 of 10 held-out failures in both arms, Fisher p = 1. No measurable effect. Worse, 2 of 10 kit-arm runs edited the gate's own guard to pass, so I then added the property suite and the vacuity guard to the protected list of the wrapper's hash manifest (not re-piloted). Kiro's Spec Correctness PBT is IDE-only and I did not use it; my properties are fast-check run by hooks. items.title: My Kiro hooks saw 5% of the writes. Here is how I found out.
items.summary: I wrote four hooks to stop Kiro from breaking my project's one rule. They fired, they blocked a bad write in a live test, and I was ready to call it done. Then I counted what they had actually seen: about 5% of the writes. This post is written as part of the Kiroween 2026 hackathon. The project is Her Hand in the Steam : Cook Mode for handwritten recipes, where the writer's own scanned hand is wiped out of the steam on a window at the step where they left a judgement. Code: github.com/edycutjong/steam . The rule the hooks were for The product's promise is "quoted, not generated". The handwriting on the glass is the scan's own ink. No handwriting font, no synthetic voice, no imitation of the hand. I turned that into steering files and into Kiro hooks: no-imitation refuses a write under src/ that speaks or fakes handwriting. catalog-gate refuses a write to the public catalog that lists a recipe failing the ingestion gate. props-on-save re-runs the gate whenever an agent saves a reading. I tested them in a live Kiro session: four writes tried, two refused (a file calling speechSynthesis , and the catalog). Both blocks are in docs/kiro-evidence/hooks.log . Good. The count Later I wrote a small tool ( tools/evidence/session-ledger.ts ) that reads Kiro's own session store for the workspace and counts, per tool call, what was written and whether a hook event followed. Across 39 sessions: 543 shell commands wrote under src/ (368 of them to non-test files). 30 write-tool calls ( fs_write , str_replace ) wrote under src/ . 0 of the 543 had a hook event. Kiro had been writing code mostly through its shell tool (heredocs, sed , python3 -c ). My hooks matched the write tools. The enforcement I had demonstrated was real, and it covered roughly 5% of the calls. The ledger's write rule is a heuristic with known misses, so treat the counts as approximate, but not as approximate as the gap. Fixing it with the spec that Kiro itself uses I made it a bugfix spec ( .kiro/specs/hook-coverage/bugfix.md ), red tests first, 12 [kiro] commits: shell-gate (PreToolUse, matcher shell ) judges the text a shell command writes under src/ with the same rules as no-imitation , and refuses any shell write of the catalog other than npm run catalog . About 0.06 s per call. src-scan-after-shell (PostToolUse, matcher shell ) judges the added lines under src/ after every shell command, so a script that builds a path from parts is still seen. About 0.11 s per call. A steering line: edit files with the write tools. { "name" : "shell-gate" , "trigger" : "PreToolUse" , "matcher" : "shell" , "action" : { "type" : "command" , "command" : "node tools/hooks/shell-gate.ts" } , "timeout" : 10 } Three live probes, each with its line in hooks.log : Probe Outcome heredoc writing speechSynthesis into src/steam/zz-shell-probe.ts refused, the file was never created echo '{}' > content/catalog.json refused, the catalog stayed byte-identical python3 -c building the path and the word from parts not seen before it ran; caught after the write by src-scan The same habit, earlier: a test that passed the bug The first defect of this kind showed up in the kill test, before the build. The prototype cropped each recipe line from the scan with boxes read by eye, and they overlapped the neighbouring lines. Handwriting does not sit in tidy rows: strokes cross between lines, so a box cut there slices letters. I turned the property into a gate (P4: a note may show only its own line's ink) and replaced boxes with ink-ownership masks built by code. Agents return line and word indices; code builds the masks; the gate decides. Run against a reproduction of those eye-read boxes the gate fails steps 1 to 5 (5 failed, 1 passed); against the ownership masks it passes. That red-to-green is the crop-overlap bugfix spec, and the two runs are in docs/kiro-evidence/crop-overlap/ . Both stories have the same shape. A check written by the same side that did the work shares its blind spot. The useful move was a second check that did not share its blind spot: a property over component ownership in one case, a count taken from the agent's own session log in the other. What still does not work In headless kiro-cli , a PostToolUse exit 2 only logs. It is not shown to the agent and does not stop it. src-scan is evidence, not a block. A script run by name, find -exec and xargs are not seen before they run. PreTaskExec and PostTaskExec hooks did not fire headless in my probe (kiro-cli 3.5.0, 5 of 7 trigger types fired), so my tests-after-task hook never ran in this project. The lesson A hook that blocks a probe is not coverage. If you enforce a rule with hooks, count what the hooks saw against what the agent did, from the agent's own session log. Mine took one afternoon to write and changed what I believed about my own setup. The rest of the Kiro evidence, including what was planned and not built (no MCP server, no Power, no spec-vs-vibe comparison), is in docs/KIRO.md and docs/EXPERIMENTS.md . Try the project: https://steam.edycu.dev

The rule the hooks were for

The product's promise is "quoted, not generated". The handwriting on the glass is the scan's own ink. No handwriting font, no synthetic voice, no imitation of the hand. I turned that into steering files and into Kiro hooks:

  • no-imitation refuses a write under src/ that speaks or fakes handwriting.
  • catalog-gate refuses a write to the public catalog that lists a recipe failing the ingestion gate.
  • props-on-save re-runs the gate whenever an agent saves a reading.

I tested them in a live Kiro session: four writes tried, two refused (a file calling speechSynthesis, and the catalog). Both blocks are in docs/kiro-evidence/hooks.log. Good.

The count

Later I wrote a small tool (tools/evidence/session-ledger.ts) that reads Kiro's own session store for the workspace and counts, per tool call, what was written and whether a hook event followed. Across 39 sessions:

  • 543 shell commands wrote under src/ (368 of them to non-test files).
  • 30 write-tool calls (fs_write, str_replace) wrote under src/.
  • 0 of the 543 had a hook event.

Kiro had been writing code mostly through its shell tool (heredocs, sed, python3 -c). My hooks matched the write tools. The enforcement I had demonstrated was real, and it covered roughly 5% of the calls. The ledger's write rule is a heuristic with known misses, so treat the counts as approximate, but not as approximate as the gap.

Fixing it with the spec that Kiro itself uses

I made it a bugfix spec (.kiro/specs/hook-coverage/bugfix.md), red tests first, 12 [kiro] commits:

  • shell-gate (PreToolUse, matcher shell) judges the text a shell command writes under src/ with the same rules as no-imitation, and refuses any shell write of the catalog other than npm run catalog. About 0.06 s per call.
  • src-scan-after-shell (PostToolUse, matcher shell) judges the added lines under src/ after every shell command, so a script that builds a path from parts is still seen. About 0.11 s per call.
  • A steering line: edit files with the write tools. 
{
  "name": "shell-gate",
  "trigger": "PreToolUse",
  "matcher": "shell",
  "action": { "type": "command", "command": "node tools/hooks/shell-gate.ts" },
  "timeout": 10
}

Three live probes, each with its line in hooks.log:

Probe Outcome heredoc writing speechSynthesis into src/steam/zz-shell-probe.ts refused, the file was never created echo '{}' > content/catalog.json refused, the catalog stayed byte-identical python3 -c building the path and the word from parts not seen before it ran; caught after the write by src-scan
The same habit, earlier: a test that passed the bug

The first defect of this kind showed up in the kill test, before the build. The prototype cropped each recipe line from the scan with boxes read by eye, and they overlapped the neighbouring lines. Handwriting does not sit in tidy rows: strokes cross between lines, so a box cut there slices letters. I turned the property into a gate (P4: a note may show only its own line's ink) and replaced boxes with ink-ownership masks built by code. Agents return line and word indices; code builds the masks; the gate decides. Run against a reproduction of those eye-read boxes the gate fails steps 1 to 5 (5 failed, 1 passed); against the ownership masks it passes. That red-to-green is the crop-overlap bugfix spec, and the two runs are in docs/kiro-evidence/crop-overlap/.

Both stories have the same shape. A check written by the same side that did the work shares its blind spot. The useful move was a second check that did not share its blind spot: a property over component ownership in one case, a count taken from the agent's own session log in the other.

What still does not work
  • In headless kiro-cli, a PostToolUse exit 2 only logs. It is not shown to the agent and does not stop it. src-scan is evidence, not a block.
  • A script run by name, find -exec and xargs are not seen before they run.
  • PreTaskExec and PostTaskExec hooks did not fire headless in my probe (kiro-cli 3.5.0, 5 of 7 trigger types fired), so my tests-after-task hook never ran in this project.
The lesson

A hook that blocks a probe is not coverage. If you enforce a rule with hooks, count what the hooks saw against what the agent did, from the agent's own session log. Mine took one afternoon to write and changed what I believed about my own setup.

The rest of the Kiro evidence, including what was planned and not built (no MCP server, no Power, no spec-vs-vibe comparison), is in docs/KIRO.md and docs/EXPERIMENTS.md.

items.title: I gave a Kiro agent a Commodore 64 and a checksum it can't argue with
items.summary: The human problem first: in 1984 you typed a program out of a magazine, hit RUN, and got ?SYNTAX ERROR IN 20 . Forty years later the page is a scan, free OCR has misread the slashed zero as an 8 , and the program is dead again. The obvious fix is to hand the listing to an LLM. The obvious failure is that it will happily return a line that runs and is wrong. This is my entry to the Kiroween 2026 hackathon (Resurrection), and it is built around one idea: the model chooses where to look; code decides what is true. Live: https://ready.edycu.dev (press Resurrect ) · Kiro view: https://ready.edycu.dev/kiro The magazine already printed the answer key COMPUTE!'s Gazette ended its program lines with a checksum comment, :rem NNN . Per line, it is the sum of the character codes of the line number and the body (spaces count 0), mod 256. So most OCR errors show up offline, without a model, as a line whose recomputed sum differs from the printed one (a matching sum is not proof the line is identical): export function computeChecksum ( lineNo : number , body : string ) : number { let sum = rawSum ( String ( lineNo ) ) ; for ( const seg of scanBody ( body ) ) { if ( seg . kind === "group" ) { if ( seg . name !== SPACE_TOKEN ) sum += TOKENS [ seg . name ] ! * seg . count ; } else if ( seg . char !== " " ) { sum += rawSum ( seg . char ) ; } } return sum % 256 ; } A Kiro spec ( checksum-oracle ) produced this, plus a tokenizer, from EARS requirements. While implementing the spec's tasks, Kiro probed the real C64 core and found three places where my own spec was wrong about how the machine behaves. The agent can propose, never write The fixer is a Kiro custom agent, resurrector . Its tool list is six MCP tools from a server I wrote ( c64_reload , c64_run , c64_read_screen , c64_press , checksum_line , apply_patch ). File read, shell, write and web are denied. The only way to change the listing is apply_patch , and a Pre Tool Use hook runs the same gate code the browser runs before the call reaches the server: // abridged from scripts/hooks/checksum-gate.mjs const v = applyPatch ( listing , patch , expected , { force_unverified : Boolean ( toolInput . force_unverified ) , refusalCounts : refusals , } ) ; // ...later: refused -> exit 2, stderr = the gate's reason, fed back to the model if ( verdict . verdict === "refused" ) { /* ... */ process . exit ( 2 ) ; } A patch is accepted only if the line is typeable on a real C64 keyboard, its checksum matches the one printed on the page, and the emulated C64 then runs it. After repeated refusals the agent may force a line, but a forced line is stamped FORCED and the verdict can never be RESURRECTED. The Cheat button on the site empties the broken line through the same gate; it is refused. The wall Kiro's Agent Stop hook is how I make the agent keep going until the program's title screen appears. It fires once per prompt, so one forced extra turn is all you get. My recorder therefore resumes the session between cycles. It works, but it is a limit I only found by measuring the hook headless ( evidence/spikes/spike-K2.md ). The second wall was credits. Two of my three feature specs reached or neared their credit caps mid-task (51.26 of 50, 68.71 of 70). I finished the ones I could with Claude Code (one task of the MCP spec is still open) and labelled them claude-direct in the commit messages and the DX report, rather than pretend Kiro wrote them. Numbers All from files in the repo: 492 tests in 41 files, including a property that types generated and OCR-mutated lines into the real C64 core and compares memory with my tokenizer. (Claude Code wrote it, not Kiro.) It found four edges (a body starting with a digit merges into the line number, for one). Gate applyPatch : p50 0.01 ms, p95 0.03 ms (N=2000). Agent evals: 7 of 9 cases run and passing, 6 of 6 model runs RESURRECTED (2 cases, N=3 each). Cases 5 and 6 are not run. Experiment E0: on the real 1984 page, plain search fixed 3 of 18 failing lines; the agent made all 18 checksum-consistent (N=2). Honest limits The live site is recorded playback. No C64 ROM is hosted (rights), so "IT LIVES" there is captioned "as recorded". The 1984 page and its OCR output are not in the repo. On the real title path the result is 19 of 28 lines source-exact against a vision-read reference; the rest are checksum-consistent, not proven identical. /scan flags checksum mismatches on live pages but withholds the repair. I did not run an experiment isolating steering's effect, so I claim none. Kiro was used through kiro-cli: three feature specs, a custom agent, four hooks, seven steering files, an MCP server, a skill. The prompts I sent, in order, are in prompts/ in the repo.
